Two insights I brought back from my trip to Dubai

After a week working there, I noticed two things that really stuck with me:

1.	The office effect.
When we were all in one room, communication was effortless. Big topics were solved in just a few hours. The productivity felt amazing.
But the downside was obvious: remote teammates were out of sync, and it created a “decoupling effect.” It showed me how powerful in-person collaboration can be, but also how hard it is to scale in a distributed setup.

2.	Thinking in English.
After a few days of speaking almost only English, I caught myself walking around and thinking in English too, even my inner dialogue switched. That immersion made me realize how much faster you grow in a language when you’re fully surrounded by it.

Both experiences gave me energy. One showed me the speed of co-located work, the other showed me how environment shapes your mindset.

👉 I’m curious: what’s the biggest shift you noticed when switching between remote and in-person work (or between different languages)?

The real question isn’t “will AI replace us?”, it’s “how do we use it?”
After 7+ years in frontend dev, here’s what I see:

🔹 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿
Treats AI like a “smart Stack Overflow”: pastes prompts, fixes bugs for hours, stitches code together. Useful, but often messy.
Stack Overflow’s 2025 survey (https://lnkd.in/dD9kDVia ) says 84% of devs use AI, but nearly half don’t trust the results. No surprise.

🔹 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁 (𝗢𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿)
Thinks in systems: data, components, user flows. Uses AI as a helper for small tasks, but keeps the bigger picture in mind.

⚙️ Backends are easier to orchestrate – logic, inputs/outputs, automated tests.

🎨 Frontends are tougher – because you carry a double load:

Data layer: APIs, state, integrations (AI can help).
User experience: smooth animations, frustration-free UX (AI can’t “feel” user irritation).

Humans still check for emotions.

🧩 𝗠𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆
The future belongs to orchestrators – especially in frontend.
It’s about engineering + empathy. That’s what keeps you valuable. 🚀

Are you still just “chatting” with AI? You’re missing 90% of its power.

AI agents aren’t about the future, they’re about how we work today.
And if you think “AI just helps write code”, you’re already behind.

👉 I broke down the entire philosophy in the carousel attached.


> The Shift: From Chaos to Workflow

To stay productive, you must stop using AI chaotically and start building repeatable systems.

Not just “ask something in a chat,” but design a process where:
- You have a Source (e.g., a call transcript).
- You provide clear requirements (in a simple text file I call it Req.md).
- The AI produces a draft (like a Summary.md).
- You act as the Validator (the crucial “Human-in-the-loop” step).
- And only then, you publish to Notion, Jira, Slack, or Email.


> My 10-Minute Sprint Report

After each sprint, I now can do this in just 10 minutes:
1. Take the list of completed tasks as a Source.
2. Use my AI workflow to generate a concise summary.
3. Validate and slightly edit the draft.
4. The system automatically stores it in Notion, drafts an email with the link, and sends a Slack notification: “Report sent, please check.”

At every step, I’m not the operator doing the routine work.
I’m the validator.


> Why This Is a Game-Changer

This isn’t an “AI toy.” It’s an operating system for your work.

Anthropic describes 5 core Workflow Patterns that perfectly align with this:
- Prompt Chaining
- Routing
- Parallelization
- Orchestrator-Workers
- Evaluator-Optimizer

📖 Full article for the curious by Anthropic - https://lnkd.in/dgBEYxKr

Once you start thinking in these terms, AI becomes a true extension of your team.


> The Call

If you’re a manager, consultant, or team lead — start building these workflows now.
Don’t wait until it becomes the new standard. By then, it will be too late.

Document the system first, then let AI build it systematically.

1. Created product-spec, functional-spec, architecture-spec
2. Detailed README for each of 4 agents with implementation roadmap  
3. Fed specs into Cursor AI for rich context
4. Versioned development: v1.0 → v1.1 → v1.2

🤖 CURSOR AI AS DEVELOPMENT PARTNER

Key pattern: Document → Context → Generate → Review → Iterate

- Converting specs into working FastAPI routes
- Generating React components from UI specifications
- Creating comprehensive test suites from functional specs  
- Implementing Docker orchestration from architecture docs

Version-based development delivered:
- v1.0.0: Core CrewAI + FastAPI architecture
- v1.1.0: NextJS frontend + Docker orchestration
- v1.2.0: WebSocket + polling fallback, auto-refresh UI

Professional practices included:
- CHANGELOG.md with detailed release notes
- Comprehensive testing with proper fixtures

Result: From documentation to production system with reliability patterns!

Documentation-First + Cursor AI + Systematic Versioning = Production-Ready AI Systems

Hands-On Hiring: Ditch the Delegation or Settle for Mediocrity

Want top-tier talent? Then roll up your sleeves and dive in personally - anything less is a recipe for regret. As a hiring manager in tech, I’ve learned the hard way: Delegating stages to three different people? That’s lazy bureaucracy, filtering out gems while letting average Joes slip through.

My method? Total immersion. I handle every step myself - from screening resumes to deep-dive interviews and final offers. It sucks up time and energy, sure, but it’s the only way to spot real diamonds: The passionate innovators, the problem-solvers who think outside the box, the ones who’ll crush KPIs without hand-holding.

Result? Every hire I’ve made this way has been a superstar - driving projects forward, boosting team morale, and delivering results that blow expectations away. HR pros and recruiters might whine about scalability, but if you’re serious about building a killer team, stop outsourcing your judgment. Own it, or own the failures.

What’s your hiring horror story? Delegation disaster or immersion triumph? Spill in the comments!

Companies will fight hard to save $50 and not notice they are wasting $5,000 doing it

A cheap tool gets treated like a major budget decision. The request turns into approval hoops, explanations, follow-ups, and waiting

Some might call this "Lean" or "being frugal." But it's actually the opposite.
True Lean thinking is about optimizing the flow of value and eliminating waste. When a company creates a $200 process to approve a $50 tool, they aren't being Lean -- they are generating Lean waste.

In a pursuit of "cost-cutting" they create massive overhead in waiting and overprocessing. The real cost shows up in:
- Lost momentum (the team stops moving while waiting for a SaaS login)
- Context switching (engineers filling out finance forms instead of coding)
- Manager touchpoints (expensive hours spent in "alignment" meetings)
- Delayed output

Most companies think that they overspending. But in reality they are overpaying for buying friction

If your control process costs more than the asset itself, you aren't saving money, you’re subsidizing inefficiency

Have you personally faced such behavior from a company in your career?

Most founders do not want engineering.

They want a vending machine for features.

Push harder.  
Scope faster.  
Ship now.  
Negotiate the timeline.

But engineering does not work like that.

The more pressure you add to a system you do not understand, the more you get:
- worse quality
- more chaos
- more churn
- less predictable delivery

Software is not a checklist.  
And deadlines do not become real just because a founder says them out loud.

If you want to sell a square table, you need to build a square table.

If you keep cutting the corners to move faster, eventually you are selling something round.

And that is not what the customer asked for.

That is what happens when companies treat engineering like a feature factory.

They do not get speed.  
They get distortion.

Real delivery speed comes from understanding constraints, sequencing work properly, and protecting quality.

Not from pushing harder.

I started as a full-stack developer 8 years ago, and initially, my job was not about building systems. It was just "add documentation" or "fix this endpoint" type of tasks.
Nowadays, if you are still doing this by hand, you are definitely doing something wrong. 

Of course, there are exceptions and exclusions, but in general - just use AI for that

Not fresh news but that’s noticeable that when AI writes code and proposes architecture, you as an “AI orchestration operator” need to sort out what is good and what is not, and to do that you need to have:

* experience in the industry to understand what is working in real life with humans across the product
* domain experience to know what problem you are trying to solve and for whom
* pattern knowledge from good old books

And the last thing is becoming more and more important each day. Since you can relatively easily understand what is working well and who your target audience is, but the language that really speeds up things and helps you communicate- is patterns.

So instead of daily saying to AI “maximize reusability and make sure that we can easily make changes in the future for feature X” - you say “use SOLID and DDD for module X” and this level of abstraction will allow you both (AI and yourself) to talk about very particular, concrete and well known things instead of speaking as a plain human - use that as advantage not as handicap

Estimates are not promises

One of the most annoying misunderstandings I see in tech is treating a software estimate as a hard commitment

We’ve all been there: you get dropped into a legacy codebase that someone else hacked together over six months. At the same time, your calendar is a minefield of recurring meetings, you’re trying to shipping a minor release on another project, and people keep dropping by with "just a quick question." Then someone asks: “When will this feature be ready?”
The honest answer is: “I have absolutely no idea.”Especially when you're dealing with third-party APIs, zero documentation, and a system where the entire context lives exclusively in one senior dev's head

But you can’t just say that. So instead of guessing a random date to make management happy, we need to treat estimates for what they actually are: hypotheses, not promises.
A realistic answer sounds more like this: "Let’s aim for Friday. That’s assuming the scope stays the same, I actually get the API keys today, and I don’t get pulled into emergency firefighting. If priorities shift, the date shifts."

This isn't pushback or being difficult. It’s just how reality works.
Uncertainty is always at its peak on day one, and you can't just "think harder" to make it disappear. As an engineer, you don't owe anyone a perfect psychic prediction. What you do owe the team is making that uncertainty visible

The math here is simple:
 - More scope = new date.
 - More meetings = less focus time.
 - No handover = discovery phase comes first

Estimates don’t exist to guarantee a perfect timeline. They exist so we can manage reality instead of just praying things work out

Your job as an engineer is not to defend the plan 

One of the biggest shifts in my career happened when I stopped treating every new, sudden request as a personal problem I had to solve, and started treating it as a trade-off I needed to explain

Early on, whenever a PM dropped a new task or an "urgent" bug into the middle of a sprint, my default reaction was: “How do I squeeze this in?” I’d work later, skip breaks, switch contexts like crazy, and just push harder. The unspoken assumption was that if I were just a "good enough" engineer, I should be able to make it work

But reality doesn’t care about your motivation. If a new requirement drops on Wednesday, and you try to absorb it through sheer stress just to save the original Friday deadline, you aren't fixing the problem. You are just making the lack of planning invisible. And you'll still feel guilty when Friday gets missed anyway.
Now, I look at it differently. I don't try to fit it in; I just ask: “What drops off the plate because of this?”

It’s not pushback, and it’s not drama. It’s just basic transparency. If we add scope, the timeline moves. If you drag me into three more alignment meetings, I have less time to actually write code. These aren't opinions, they're just consequences.
A lot of devs think that setting boundaries means constantly shouting "no" at management. It's usually much simpler: you don't refuse the work, you just explain its actual cost. Once that cost is out in the open, let the business decide if they actually want to pay it

Ironically, this creates way less conflict. You’re no longer fighting over priorities. You are just showing people how resources work. Projects rarely fail because someone had bad intentions; they fail because everyone pretended constraints didn't exist until production broke

(One more cat’s photo 😸)

Stop trying to absorb infinite work

There is a dangerous illusion floating around right now: the idea that because we have AI tools, an engineer’s capacity has suddenly become infinite.
It usually starts with management noticing how fast tasks get closed, followed by the inevitable: “Hey, since AI speeds things up, can you quickly jump into this other project? And also join this alignment meeting? Oh, and we need to accelerate the next release.” Individual requests sound harmless, but the mistake devs still make is trying to absorb it all without asking the obvious question: “What are we deprioritizing in exchange?”

Here is the cold truth: AI increases throughput, not capacity
Yes, a single engineer today can produce significantly more output than three years ago. We generate code faster, spin up multiple agents, build prototypes in minutes, and vomit out documentation in seconds. But every single agent and automated script produces artifacts. And at the end of the day, someone still has to understand them, validate the business logic, and take actual responsibility for the production outcome

In 99% of teams, that "someone" is still a human.
A few years ago, the main bottleneck in software engineering was literally writing the code. Today, the bottleneck has shifted to decision-making. It’s about understanding context, evaluating high-level trade-offs, and knowing where the system will break if we cut corners. You can spin up ten more agents, but you’ll just choke your senior devs with code reviews and verification tasks

That’s why ignoring constraints doesn’t make them disappear. It just moves the bottleneck.
Over the years, I’ve stopped saying "that's impossible" when new work flies in. Instead, the response is simple: "If X becomes Priority #1, which existing priority moves down?". I’m not trying to dodge the work. I just want everyone to be clear on what we’re breaking or delaying if we take this on

At the end of the day, engineering has always been about managing constraints. AI just made the code cheaper, but human focus is more expensive than ever

(Another cat picture for attention attraction 😁)

Silence Is Agreement

One of the most expensive mistakes engineers make is assuming management can automatically see their constraints

They can’t

If you don’t explicitly call out a lack of time, shifting priorities, or missing information, leadership will naturally assume you have enough of all three

In most companies, silence is interpreted as agreement

Not because managers are evil or incompetent. Everyone is just operating with incomplete data. If you see an unrealistic deadline or a conflicting priority and choose to stay quiet, you’re implicitly signing up for the burnout

The math here is simple. Early warning means plenty of options to fix the course. Late warning means firefighting and missed expectations

If something is broken, speak up early. It’s not complaining; it’s giving your team a chance to pivot

Complaining vs Escalating

Complaining and escalating often sound similar, but they land completely differently in a manager’s ears

Complaining sounds like: “This deadline is unrealistic” Or “We just don’t have enough people”

Escalating sounds like: “This deadline is unrealistic. We either need to cut the scope by 30% or pull in another engineer, otherwise we’ll miss the release”

The first approach just transfers your frustration. The second transfers actionable information

One might get you some sympathy, but only the other creates action. Your goal shouldn’t be to convince everyone that your job is hard, it’s to make the necessary trade-offs visible so people can make a choice

Problems vs Decisions

Most engineers are brilliant at identifying problems. Fewer are good at tracking down root causes. But very few actually know how to turn those problems into decisions.

Think about how it sounds in meetings:

The Problem: “We don’t have enough people.” (An observation)

The Diagnosis: “The release is at risk because we don’t have enough people.” (Better, shows impact)

The Decision: “We need either one additional engineer or a two-week deadline extension.” (Perfect)

Companies don’t pay the highest salaries for finding problems. They pay for reducing uncertainty.

The most valuable people in the room aren’t the ones who build the longest list of issues. They’re the ones who look at a messy situation and answer a simple question:

“What should we do next?”

Explanation vs Ownership

There’s a massive gap between explaining a failure and taking ownership of it

Explanations sound reasonable:

“The requirements changed.”
“The engineer was reassigned.”
“We didn’t have enough resources.”

But explanations only describe reality. Ownership changes it. Taking ownership means you immediately pair the context with a decision:

“The requirements changed, so the old estimate is no longer valid. Here is the revised timeline.”
“We are short-staffed. To hit the date, we either need to drop Feature X or bring in help.”

The most valuable people I’ve worked with weren’t the ones who could explain every problem. They were the ones who could turn uncertainty into a choice

A few weeks ago we spent several hours discussing what looked like a tiny issue in one of our AI voice agents. It wasn’t hallucinating, the latency was fine, conversations were coherent, but every now and then it would address a female patient using masculine forms.

From an engineering perspective, that’s an almost boring bug. It’s easy to look at it and think, “We’ll fix it eventually.” But that’s not how users experience software. They don’t evaluate prompt quality, model architecture or response latency. They simply notice that something feels wrong, and once trust is gone, they stop caring how technically impressive the system is.

It reminded me that engineering quality and product quality aren’t always the same thing. We spend a lot of time optimizing metrics that users never see, while the details they notice are often the ones that determine whether they trust the product at all.

I’ve been thinking about how my job has changed over the years.

Earlier in my career, most of my mental energy went into technical decisions. Choosing frameworks, comparing libraries, researching tools, evaluating trade-offs between technologies, figuring out which approach would still make sense two years later. I’d say around 80% of my work was technical and maybe 20% was focused on the product itself.

Today it feels almost reversed.

Most of my time is spent thinking about users, product behavior, safety, evaluation, edge cases, and whether we’re solving the right problem in the first place. The implementation still matters, but AI has significantly reduced the cognitive load of many day-to-day technical decisions. Instead of spending hours comparing libraries or writing boilerplate, I’m reviewing solutions, setting direction, and validating whether the result actually solves the problem.

There are still moments when deep technical work becomes essential. Greenfield projects, new infrastructure, foundational architectural decisions—those still require careful engineering. But they’re exceptions rather than the default.

Looking back, I don’t think engineering has become less technical. I think the center of gravity has shifted. Less effort goes into choosing the right tools, and much more goes into asking the right questions.

Yesterday I listened to an interview with Andrey Doronichev . One idea from the conversation stayed with me. Andrey argued that the biggest bottleneck for AI is no longer the technology itself, but the last mile: convincing a 70-year-old dentist that AI belongs in their clinic and  can genuinely improve the way they work.

That resonated with me because it’s surprisingly close to what I do every day. At Sully.ai , I work on AI receptionists for healthcare providers, and while building the system is an interesting engineering challenge, getting it to fit naturally into a real clinic is often the harder problem.

The technical side is only one piece of the puzzle. The system has to earn trust, integrate into existing workflows, handle edge cases gracefully, and behave consistently enough that people are comfortable relying on it with real patients. That’s where a lot of the real work happens.

Listening to the interview made me realize that I don’t really think of my job as “building AI” anymore. I think of it as helping bring AI into industries where people have established ways of working and very little tolerance for mistakes. The technology is impressive, but adoption is ultimately a human problem.

It made me curious whether other people working on AI products have experienced the same shift. Has the biggest challenge in your work become the technology itself, or everything that comes after it?

If you are still using AI only to write code, you are probably working somewhere around 2022 or 2023

I don’t mean that Cursor or ChatGPT are useless. They are obviously useful. But opening a chat, pasting a task, generating a function and then reviewing it is a very small part of what an engineer actually does

Most of the work is not writing code

It is understanding what the client actually asked for, finding what was discussed in Slack, checking whether the ticket still reflects the current requirements, reading old decisions in Notion or Google Docs, looking at logs, finding the relevant code, checking existing pull requests, understanding who owns the next step and making sure the result can actually be shipped

If your AI only has access to the repository, it knows almost none of this

My setup is closer to having one entry point into the whole engineering environment

It has access to the codebase, GitHub, Linear, Slack, Notion, Google Docs, Grafana and logs. The permissions are separated where they need to be separated, but the important part is that the agent can combine information from all of these systems

So instead of asking it to write some isolated piece of code, I can give it a real task

A client mentioned a problem during a meeting. The agent can find the notes, compare them with the current Linear ticket, look through the relevant Slack discussions, check the logs, trace the problem in the codebase and prepare a fix with tests and a pull request

You can also split the work between multiple agents. One investigates the logs, another checks product context, another reviews the code, another looks for previous decisions. They do not even have to use the same model

You can build your own skills and workflows around this as well. For example, how incidents should be investigated, how tickets should be reviewed, what checks are required before release or how documentation should be prepared

After some time, this becomes an environment built specifically around the way you work

And honestly, none of this requires some huge internal AI platform. In many cases it is just integrations, permissions, a few reusable skills and the willingness to automate things that you currently do manually across fifteen different tabs

The gap between this and simply asking ChatGPT to write code is enormous

It is roughly the difference between using AI as autocomplete and using it as an interface to the company’s actual engineering context

I noticed a slightly weird thing about how I react to positive feedback.

When someone tells me I did a good job, I rarely think: great, now I should do even more of this.

Usually I think: okay, so this is enough.

Now I know the bar.

And once I know the bar, I start thinking about how to reach the same result with less effort.

If it took me eight hours, next time I will try to do it in six. Then maybe in four.

Not because I want to do worse or cut corners. I just no longer need to spend time figuring out whether the result is good enough.

Before that, I can easily overdo things. Add extra checks, polish details nobody asked for, think through edge cases that probably do not matter.

Then someone says: this is good.

And for me that is not really praise. It is information.

It means I now have a pattern that works.

And if a pattern works, I can simplify it, automate part of it, give some of it to agents, or at least stop solving the same problem from zero every time.

This is probably why vague feedback is so annoying.

“Be more proactive.”

“Show more ownership.”

Okay, but what exactly worked? What result are we trying to repeat?

Give me one concrete example of work that was valuable, and I can optimize around it.

Give me a vague principle, and I will probably spend twice as much time guessing what you meant.

A super-productive employee is a curse, not a blessing.

Right now startups and companies are at the peak of wanting to hire A-players, and preferably people who are also FDE Fullstack+DevOps, empowered by AGI. But I think this becomes a dead end when the whole system starts depending on that one person.

Let’s imagine that we have a $500k budget. We can hire, for example, 1 person who will be that exact FDE Fullstack+DevOps empowered by AGI, including token costs in this budget. Or we can hire 5 people who are good at one specific thing, basically a good old agile team: 1 BE, 1 FE, 1 FullStack, 1 QA, 1 Team Lead.

And here is the question, which system seems more resilient to you? To me, the second one. Steve Jobs famously believed that a small team of A-players could run circles around a giant team of B and C players. I think there is a problem with that idea. Your job as a company manager is to use the budget as efficiently as possible. And if you bet on one rockstar, then in the best case you end up in something close to quasi-slavery to that rockstar, and in the worst case you create a single point of failure for the business. While in the second system you will have to put effort into management, but at the same time the system will be harder to break.

You may object, “Hey, but I’m not going to hire just anyone! I’ll find a person I can trust!” And I would answer, “Yes, you can, but even then you will spend resources trying to find that exact rockstar, and I’ll remind you that by nature they are a very rare animal, and right now an even scarcer resource on the job market. And even if you find them, they can get sick, they can burn out, or they can simply get hit by a bus. What are you going to do then?”

That’s why I think it’s possible to find a solution that is good enough. Because not everyone needs a rockstar, everyone needs to multiply their investment, and that is hard to do if the foundation of your system is fragile.

RimWorld is the best engineering management simulator on the market.

Look at the screenshot below. If you've played the game, you know this screen all too well. If you haven't: this is how you manage a colony.
You don't directly control individual pawns. You design an operating model: toggle manual priorities (1 to 4), configure work types, set resource boundaries, and establish constraints.

And then you watch your system fail.
 - Your best builder spends half the day hauling a single piece of wood across the map instead of finishing critical defenses before a raid.
 - Your top doctor is on the verge of a Mental Break from exhaustion because they're assigned to everything.
 - Production grinds to a halt because a single dependency is stuck in an unorganized stockpile.
 - Everyone is technically busy 100% of the time, yet nothing of actual value gets delivered.
Sound familiar?

When this happens, the knee-jerk reaction is micromanagement: right-click the pawn, force the job, override the queue. It puts out the fire for 30 seconds, but it solves nothing long-term.
Of course, real engineers aren’t RimWorld pawns. They have judgment, motivation, and the ability to challenge bad decisions.
And that’s precisely where engineering management becomes far more interesting than the game.

The goal isn’t to program people to follow a priority matrix blindly. It’s to build an environment where they have enough context, autonomy, and shared understanding to make the right decisions without constant intervention.

A good engineering leader doesn’t optimize how many tasks people complete. They design a system where people can consistently deliver valuable outcomes under real-world constraints.
And perhaps the most important lesson from RimWorld. 

So, if your organization only survives because you manually draft people and override their queues every 30 seconds, then you haven’t built a functioning team. You’ve built a single point of failure around yourself.

Overpromising might be one of the most underrated career skills in management

I’m starting to suspect that being realistic about what your team can deliver is sometimes a competitive disadvantage

Think about it

One manager promises a 10x productivity improvement. Another says 20–30% is achievable, explains the trade-offs, and builds a plan around it

A year later, both deliver 20%

Who gets more recognition?

You’d expect the second manager. They understood the problem, made a reasonable prediction, and delivered what they promised.

But I’ve seen enough to question that assumption

The first manager can still celebrate a 20% improvement, blame the remaining gap on execution, and introduce an even more ambitious plan for next quarter

And somehow, the original 10x promise disappears from the conversation

I’ve been on the engineering side of this. Turning ambitious ideas into estimates, dependencies, and executable plans, only to repeat the exercise a week later when another brilliant priority appeared

What bothers me isn’t ambition or even unrealistic predictions. Both are inevitable when building something new

It’s how easily we let people replace accountability for yesterday’s promises with excitement about tomorrow’s

At some point, I have to wonder: Are we promoting people who are good at delivering results, or people who are good at managing the perception of results?

Stop using LLMs as the world’s most expensive if-statements

We’ve become so obsessed with text generation that we’ve started treating every engineering problem as a prompt engineering problem:
Need to route an agent workflow? Call an LLM.
Any sort of classification? Call an LLM.
Filter noise or detect anomaly? Call an LLM

Need to predict tomorrow's demand? You guessed it. It’s 🪄LLM 

And then we act surprised when our systems end up slow, non-deterministic, and burning thousands of dollars on token billing.

The hype around TypeSafe’s Jev is a healthy reminder: AI is much bigger than autoregressive text generation

Here are 6 specialized models that belong in a modern AI engineering toolbox:
1. Jev (TypeSafe) -  Discrete decisions, not tokens
Instead of generating conversational text just to branch logic, it outputs calibrated, structured predictions.
Best for: Agent routing, intent classification, and next-best-action selection.
2. SAM 2 (Meta) is zero-shot spatial & temporal tracking
Prompt it with a point or box, and it segments/tracks that object across video frames with sub-pixel precision.
Best for: Visual automation, video editing pipelines, and robotics.
3. CLIP (OpenAI) - joint vision-language embeddings
Maps images and natural language into the same latent space without generating a single word.
Best for: Semantic multimodal search, zero-shot tagging, and catalog deduplication.
4. TimesFM (Google) - zero-shot time-series forecasting
A foundation model built specifically for sequential numerical data, not dialogue.
Best for: Infrastructure load forecasting, supply chain predictions, and capacity planning.
5. DeepFilterNet - acoustic signal processing
A lightweight deep neural network designed to suppress background noise in speech streams in real time.
Best for: Voice agent pre-processing, clean ASR input, and edge telecommunications.
6. DINOv2 (Meta) - self-supervised visual features
Extracts powerful, task-agnostic visual representations directly from raw pixels.
Best for: Visual similarity search, defect detection, and clustering without fine-tuning.

Note that I’m not saying that LLMs are bad.
The point is that text generation is a terrible tool for binary logic, signal cleaning, spatial tracking, and deterministic routing.
Sometimes you need to draft an email,or you just need a probability vector, a bounding box, or an embedding, and sometimes you just need a standard XGBoost model

Good AI architecture always was about how many of them you can replace with the right specialized model or eliminate entirely

What non-generative model is currently saving your team the most latency or money?

On Thursday, an internal debate completely derailed our sync:

The technical gap between a Junior and a Senior dev is basically gone.

Two years ago, I could spot seniority in 10 minutes. Seniors knew the weird edge cases in the framework, wrote clean boilerplate without googling, and didnt panic when an API failed.

Today? A junior with Cursor cranks out typed React components, mocks endpoints, and sets up Docker faster than I can review the PR. The syntax part of the job has been completely commoditized.

The real gap now is entirely product judgment.

A junior builds whatever was written in the ticket. It works, tests pass, but it’s completely unnecessary and solves the wrong problem.

A senior looks at the same ticket and asks: «Why are we touching this endpoint at all if 80% of our churn comes from the onboarding flow?»One writes code because the sprint started.

The other deletes half the requirements to protect the product.

If youre still paying senior salaries just for raw technical execution, youre basically paying $150k for an interface to Claude.

How much of your evaluation of seniors right now is still about tech trivia vs actually understanding what not to build?

Every engineering estimate is actually two numbers disguised as one:
1) How long it takes to build if nothing unexpected happens.
2) How much we still dont know about the legacy code were about to touch.

Founders always hear the first number and put it on the investor slide.
Engineers always mean the second number and pad it by 2x just to survive the sprint.
Stop asking «when will it be done?» on day one. Ask «whats the one unknown that could blow this up from 3 days to 3 weeks, and how do we test it before noon tomorrow?»

The most expensive phrase in an engineering architecture review isn't just "I disagree"; it's not what worries me in an architecture review. What worries me is 45 minutes of polite silence followed by "LGTM, let’s ship it."


When seniors stop arguing in design docs, they haven't reached alignment — they've just checked out because pushing back feels pointless.

I'd rather spend an hour refereeing a heated debate on Tuesday than spend three months rewriting a polite compromise in production.

When was the last time someone on your team actually killed a bad feature in a design review?

Everyone brags about how their team writes code 3x faster with AI now.

Nobody mentions what happened to their PR queue.

Writing code was never the real bottleneck. Understanding it was.
Before Cursor and Claude, if a developer wanted to ship a messy 800-line PR, it at least took them three days to type it out. You had natural friction.

Now anyone on the team can generate 1,000 lines of plausible-looking code before lunch. It compiles, the happy-path test passes, and then it lands on a senior engineers desk. And that's where velocity goes to die. Reviewing code you didn't write is 5x harder than generating it. When half of that PR was written by an LLM that doesn't understand your domain invariants, code review turns into forensic archaeology.

We didn't eliminate the bottleneck. We just moved it from typing to reviewing — and silently turned our best engineers into full-time human linters. 

Our rule now is simple: if you can't explain every architectural trade-off in your PR in two sentences without looking at the diff, it gets closed without review.

How are you handling the PR flood in your teams right now? Stricter size limits, or changing how reviews work entirely?

Last month I watched a team spend two weeks wiring up a multi-agent workflow to route incoming customer tickets.

Three prompts, a vector store, retry logic, and a $400 monthly token bill.

It had a 12-second latency and still hallucinated on edge cases every Friday afternoon.
Yesterday someone replaced the whole thing with 25 lines of TypeScript and three if/else statements. Latency dropped to 0ms. Accuracy hit 100%. Maintenance cost: zero.

Right now, half the industry is using LLMs for deterministic routing just so they can put «agentic architecture» on the roadmap slide. But using an LLM where a regular if/else or SQL query works it is just paying OpenAI to roll dice in production, not solve the real problem.
My rule for any AI feature now: exhaust regular deterministic code first. Only bring in an agent for the messy 10% of the problem that you literally cannot write a regex or state machine for.

AI agents helped developers write 30% more code. The companies in this study didn't ship more.

A new Harvard paper by Chen and Stratton looks at 300 million work events across around 700 firms and 700,000 engineers, from 2021 to 2026. It uses GitHub, Jira, and calendar activity, not survey responses.

With AI assistants, commits rose 9% and pull requests 5%. With agents, the increases were bigger: 30% more lines of code, 20% more commits, and 23% more pull requests.

But resolved Jira issues and epics barely changed. Employment didn't move either.

The extra work seems to have landed in review. After agent adoption, PR review time rose 49%, PRs with requested changes nearly doubled, and comments per PR went up 35%. Another 14% of engineers got pulled into review work.

That makes sense when you remember engineers spend only 30-40% of their time writing code. Speeding up that part won't make reviews, verification, or deployment move any faster.

I see teams adopt Copilot or Claude Code, get a burst of output, then wonder why cycle time hasn't changed. Sometimes the review queue is the reason. The coding tool sped up one step; the rest of the process stayed the same.

Before celebrating another jump in code volume, I'd look at review capacity. In your team, what became the bottleneck after AI coding tools arrived?

Three hours of a recent call went into bargaining over estimates. The work behind those numbers stayed the same size.

I sat through one of these. A startup CEO joined a technical call and started bargaining over the engineers' estimates, one by one.

Three hours later, we had covered about 40% of the estimates. Working afterwards was hard; the feeling in the room was that we'd been had, the hours skimmed off us.

The CEO, as far as I could tell, was pleased with how far he had moved the numbers.

What shrank in that room was the buffer for being wrong — the one part of an estimate you actually miss when reality shows up.

And there's a second cost I think founders underweight. A team that watches its estimates get bargained learns, fairly quickly, that estimates here are opening positions. 

So the next ones come in padded, and now the numbers you're negotiating are worse numbers.

The fair version of the other side: pushing back is sometimes right. Estimates can be padded, or built on scope nobody has questioned yet. If a number surprises you, asking why is your job.

But that's a question about the work. Three hours spent arguing a figure is not that question.

When a number genuinely needs to come down, I think the honest move is to cut scope. Remove work, and the estimate follows it down on its own. That's a real reduction.

Single-turn benchmarks reward the exact habit that makes an AI agent annoying to work with: guessing what you meant on the first try.



We tend to assume a model that scores well on a benchmark will do well in our product. With agents, that link breaks.



A one-shot test gives the model one prompt and grades the first answer. To score well, it has to fill in everything you left out and hand back a finished-looking reply immediately.



That’s the opposite of what I want from an agent. I don’t need a tool that speculates for me. I need it to run the loop: inspect actual state, ask when critical context is missing instead of guessing, and complete the task over several turns.



The multi-turn eval piece I read this week was a vendor’s own blog - and they sell the alternative, so discount it accordingly - but their list of failure modes still reads true to me: contradictions, infinite loops, false task completion. None of those surface on turn one.



Single-turn evals are still cheap, reproducible, and fine for narrow capabilities that genuinely are one-shot. Not every task needs an agent loop, and multi-turn evals take real effort to build and maintain.



So the shift I’d suggest is smaller than throwing away your eval suite: for anything that behaves like an agent, grade the end of the loop - whether the task actually got done - instead of grading turn one in isolation.



If the first reply looks complete, that may be exactly the problem.

Trying to fix an unstable AI agent with a 200-line system prompt is like debugging a broken interface by writing longer comments



Most teams still treat prompt engineering as the main lever. In practice, the majority of hallucinations, infinite loops, and failed tool calls do not come from insufficient instructions. They come from missing contracts



When an agent gets an unpredictable payload, a bloated schema, or a polluted context, failure rates compound fast. We end up writing paragraphs of natural language to paper over what should have been enforced at the interface



Three rules that actually keep production agents stable:

1/ Strict contracts instead of verbose descriptions.

Tool specs (MCP or custom) should be minimal and strongly typed. The fewer optional fields the model has to invent, the more deterministic the run becomes.

2/ Context isolation.

Dumping full conversation history or raw database rows into one window is an anti-pattern. The agent should see only the exact state required for the current step. Everything else is noise.

3/ Structured error recovery.

A model should never have to guess why a tool call failed. Clear, actionable error states bring it back on track far better than blind retries.



Designing interfaces for LLMs follows the same principles as designing distributed systems.

If the boundaries are broken, no amount of clever prompting will save them.

In the 1920s, a Soviet filmmaker figured out something we’re still struggling with in AI.



Lev Kuleshov took the same shot of an actor with a blank expression and cut it together with three different scenes, a bowl of soup, a dead child and a woman lying on a sofa, and people saw hunger, grief and desire, even though the actor’s face never changed.



The meaning wasn’t in the face itself, it came from what people saw around it.



Something similar happens with LLMs, where the same token can be interpreted very differently depending on the surrounding context, and while self-attention is obviously more complicated than film editing, I think the comparison is useful when building agents.



When an agent fails, the first thing we usually do is give it more context: more chat history, more logs, more tool definitions, more instructions, and if that doesn’t help, maybe a bigger context window will.



But I’ve seen agents fail with all the information they needed already in the prompt, and the problem wasn’t that something was missing, it was that the important parts were buried under everything else.



A 2-million-token context window doesn’t solve this problem by itself, it just gives you more room to put things the model might not need, while the one constraint that actually matters for the next action gets lost somewhere in the middle.



I think we still treat context engineering too much like a storage problem, when a lot of the work is really about deciding what the model should see at a particular step, what can be removed without losing anything important, and which pieces of information are actually going to change its decision.



You can give an agent access to almost everything and it can still make a stupid decision, because having the information available and using it at the right moment are two very different things.

Three stories from this week's AI engineering news look unrelated. I think they're the same mistake: treating what a model produced, or remembered, as trusted input.

1. Slopsquatting. Models invent package names that don't exist, and attackers register those names on npm and PyPI. The problem is real, but I don't think it needs a new tool. A lockfile plus a human look at every new dependency in review closes most of it. The gap is teams that let an agent add dependencies with nobody looking.

2. Memory poisoning. An agent reads an email or a web page, part of it lands in long-term memory, and next session it comes back as a fact. I still want agents with memory. What I want from that memory is provenance: "the user told me" and "I read it in an inbound email" should never carry the same weight.

3. LLM reviewers you can't rely on. We hit a version of this recently. Our review agent misread its task and ended up comparing long-lived subagents instead of checking what it was asked to check. A second model grading the first wouldn't have caught that.

So I'm building a harness around our agents and wiring in Harness² from Google Research. It runs variations of a harness on the same task and refines it from the differences between executions, with no ground-truth answer needed. The hope is that it catches a misread task before it turns into a verdict, and that the agent swarm improves step by step instead of through me rewriting prompts. It's too early to say whether it works.

The common thread: a model's output is a claim. Something deterministic, or a person, decides whether it gets in.

Which of these have you actually run into in production?

The team behind Claude Code deletes most of Claude Code's prompt every time a new model ships. I think it's the most useful thing they've said this year.



Boris Cherny, who leads Claude Code, said on stage that for Opus 5 they cut more than 80% of the system prompt. With each new model they run an ablation: delete the whole prompt, bring it back line by line, keep only what changes behaviour.



The harness was never the product. It's something you re-derive for every model.



Last week I tried to automate that re-derivation at YAGNI, where agent teams take engineering tickets to a merged pull request. The plan: let a self-improving harness loop (Harness²) propose edits to our agent's skill and prompts, test them on real tickets, keep what wins.



I froze it after the first smoke runs. Every failure we found (a model's chatty preamble becoming a commit message, 18 minutes spent looking for a browser the sandbox didn't have, a verification step overrunning its clock) was an environment or code bug, found by reading logs. None of them was a prompt edit a search would discover. And one full run costs $2–5 and ~30 minutes, so separating a real improvement from noise takes dozens of runs per variant.



What we do instead: save every run's transcript, cut it at the turn where things went wrong, and replay from there with the current skill and with the proposed edit. Cents and minutes instead of dollars and half an hour, and each edit is tested at the exact decision it's meant to change.



My takeaway: before you let a model rewrite your harness, read your logs. Most of what looks like a prompt problem isn't one.



And if your CLAUDE.md has been growing since last year, it's probably encoding fixes for a model you no longer use.

I got "hacked."

This was back when I was running engineering, before AI started breaking the internet at scale. Probably a textbook case.

An email arrived: "Dear Gleb, I have found a vulnerability on your website and I am ready to use it."

A few emails later it turned out there really was a hole, just not the one I expected. A guy from Pakistan had found a way to sign up on our site endlessly. No bot farm. An old laptop and some script.

I refused to pay. It didn't seem valuable enough for a bounty.

So he scaled up. Within a week we had about 20,000 new users, and our customer support specialist's phone was blowing up, because it pinged him for every new signup.

In the end we banned his IP, and that was it.

Would you have paid him?
